blocks.text: Then her voice broke. "Mom, it's me. It's Megan."

I hadn't heard my daughter's voice in nine years. When she was twenty-two, she dropped out of college and moved across the state with a man I didn't trust. I said things I shouldn't have. She said things back. Then she changed her number, and that was that. The only one of us she still talked to was my sister, Joan.

Megan had been working as the restaurant's bookkeeper for two years. The man was long gone. She'd gone back to school at night and finished her accounting degree. She'd wanted to call me a hundred times. She never knew how to start.
So she and Joan planned it together. Joan's retirement dinner was the cover.

Megan reserved the private room under my name, ordered my favorite lemon cake, and asked the owner, Tony, to have a waiter bring us back there for dessert. The photo in the reservation was one she'd taken herself last winter, from her car outside my house, where she'd sat for an hour and couldn't make herself knock. She'd attached it so the staff would know who I was.

The waiter with the silver tray was carrying the cake. But when Megan saw me through the doorway, laughing with Joan, she panicked. She ran out the back door and quit by text that night. Joan, who didn't know what had happened, assumed the plan had been called off and didn't bring me back. And Tony, flustered, ran the room deposit through on the card I'd used to pay for dinner.
When my review went up, Tony was terrified I'd find out about the surprise before Megan was ready.

We met at the restaurant the following Saturday, in the private room. Tony refunded the four hundred dollars and brought out a new lemon cake. Megan and I didn't eat much of it. We talked until they closed.
I deleted the one-star review and wrote a new one. Five stars. "Slow service. Worth the wait."
Megan is back at the restaurant now, too. Tony rehired her the next week.
